reference.source: Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics / standard medical genetics references
clinicalPearls: Common features include short stature, characteristic facies, congenital heart disease, and a broad or webbed neck
Facial features evolve with age but classically include hypertelorism, downslanting palpebral fissures, ptosis, and low-set posteriorly rotated ears
Pulmonary valve stenosis is the most characteristic cardiac lesion, and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy also occurs
A pectus deformity (carinatum superiorly and excavatum inferiorly) and cubitus valgus are typical skeletal findings
A bleeding tendency from coagulation factor deficiencies or platelet dysfunction may complicate surgery
Belongs to the RASopathy group caused by mutations that dysregulate the RAS-MAPK signalling pathway, most commonly in PTPN11
Cryptorchidism is common in affected males and may affect fertility
Development is usually normal or only mildly affected, distinguishing it from many other syndromes
reference.pathophysiology: Noonan syndrome is one of the RASopathies, a family of disorders caused by germline mutations that increase signalling through the RAS-mitogen-activated protein kinase (RAS-MAPK) pathway, which governs cell proliferation, differentiation, and survival. The most frequent gene involved is PTPN11, with additional cases attributed to SOS1, RAF1, RIT1, KRAS, and others. Excess pathway activity during development produces the cardiac defects, characteristic facial and skeletal features, growth restriction, and haematological abnormalities. Inheritance is autosomal dominant with variable expressivity, and many cases arise de novo.
additionalDifferentials: Other RASopathies such as cardiofaciocutaneous and Costello syndromes
additionalInvestigations: Molecular genetic panel testing for RASopathy-associated genes
Echocardiography and electrocardiography to characterise cardiac involvement
Coagulation screen and platelet studies, particularly before surgery
Growth monitoring and endocrine assessment for short stature
Renal ultrasound and developmental assessment as indicated
redFlags: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy that may progress and cause heart failure or arrhythmia
Unexpected bleeding during surgery or trauma from an underlying coagulopathy
Rare association with juvenile myelomonocytic leukaemia, especially in certain genotypes
Significant feeding difficulties and failure to thrive in infancy
reference.prognosis: Most individuals have a good long-term outlook with normal or near-normal cognition, though prognosis is influenced by the severity of cardiac disease, particularly hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
pitfalls: Overlooking the diagnosis in a child with short stature and pulmonary stenosis
Failing to check coagulation before invasive procedures
Attributing the phenotype in a female to Turner syndrome without genetic testing
Not monitoring for evolving hypertrophic cardiomyopathy over time
management: Treat the characteristic pulmonary valve stenosis with balloon valvuloplasty or surgical repair, and monitor for and manage hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
Consider growth hormone therapy for short stature after endocrine assessment
Screen coagulation and platelet function before any surgery and manage the bleeding tendency proactively
Provide developmental support and educational intervention for learning and motor delays
Undertake regular cardiac surveillance with echocardiography and electrocardiography given the risk from hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
Offer genetic counselling for this autosomal dominant RASopathy, with molecular confirmation and assessment of relatives
Coordinate multidisciplinary care across cardiology, endocrinology, clinical genetics and developmental services
